content: Industrial microbiology, also known as microbial biotechnology, involves the utilization of microorganisms in the production of food and industrial products. When microorganisms are used to produce food for human or animal consumption, this application is often categorized under food microbiology. The microorganisms employed in industrial processes can be naturally occurring isolates, laboratory-selected mutants, or genetically engineered organisms. In the realm of food microbiology, industrial microbiology processes are responsible for the production of various products, including yogurt, cheese, chocolate, butter, pickles, sauerkraut, soy sauce, vitamins, amino acids, microbial polysaccharides (used as food thickeners), alcohol, sausages, and silage (animal feed). The role of beneficial bacteria, such as probiotics, is becoming increasingly significant in the food industry. Microorganisms are also capable of producing a wide array of biopolymers, such as polysaccharides, polyesters, and polyamides. These biopolymers can range from viscous solutions to materials resembling plastics. Advances in genetic engineering have enabled the production of biopolymers with customized material properties, making them suitable for high-value medical applications, including tissue engineering and drug delivery. Industrial microbiology facilitates the biosynthesis of compounds such as xanthan, alginate, cellulose, cyanophycin, poly(gamma-glutamic acid), levan, hyaluronic acid, organic acids, oligosaccharides, polysaccharides, and polyhydroxyalkanoates. Microbial biodegradation plays a critical role in bioremediation, which involves the breakdown of pollutants to clean up contaminated environments. Microorganisms can degrade substances such as oil, polychlorinated biphenyls (PCBs), polyaromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs), pharmaceutical compounds, radionuclides, and metals. In waste biotreatment, microorganisms are employed to process the vast quantities of waste generated by modern societies. Biotreatment, which uses living organisms to treat waste, is an environmentally friendly, relatively simple, and cost-effective alternative to traditional physico-chemical cleanup methods. Confined environments, such as bioreactors, can be utilized in these biotreatment processes. In healthcare and medicine, microorganisms are used to produce biological products for humans and animals, such as insulin, growth hormones, and antibodies. Diagnostic assays employing monoclonal antibodies, DNA probe technology, or real-time PCR are used as rapid tests to detect pathogenic organisms in clinical laboratories. The study of extremophiles—microorganisms that thrive in extreme conditions such as high temperatures, high salinity, low pH, or high radiation—has led to the discovery of microbes with novel capabilities that can be harnessed for industrial purposes. Corynebacteria represent a diverse group of Gram-positive bacteria found in various ecological niches, including soil, vegetables, sewage, skin, and cheese smear. Among them, Corynebacterium glutamicum holds immense industrial significance and is one of the most biotechnologically important bacterial species. It is responsible for the annual production of over two million tons of amino acids, primarily L-glutamate and L-lysine. The genome sequence of C. glutamicum has been published, providing valuable insights into its genetic and metabolic capabilities.
